Oh man, this question is right in my wheelhouse. Handbrake and MakeMKV go together like peanut butter and jelly. If you're looking for software to view your ripped media, check out Plex.
I believe this is the best answer. Make MKV should still be available for free. But I loved them do much that I bought the software. Haven't bought a movie since.

Agreed :) and yes, still free during the beta (you just have to reenter the beta key every few months) but I just bought it outright as well. Handbrake + MakeMKV + Plex is a commonly recommended trio for ripping DVD/BluRay, and for good reason. They'll also all run on Linux. I have them set up on my Fedora desktop.

I've ripped my 1800+ DVD collection (not including the TV shows) and recently started doing Blu-Ray as well, and I've not had a problem with any of them.

Thank you! I was able to use MakeMKV and Handbrake to successfully rip a Blu-Ray. One question though - the finished file was over 8GB (The Fifth Element @ 1080). Is there a step I'm missing to compress the file to ~2GB?

My Blu-Rays are usually about 4-6 GB at 1080p, so that's not too far off. Blu-Ray usually starts at 20-40GB and shrinks down to 4-6. DVD usually starts at 8 and shrink to 1-2.

As long as you're converting the MKV rips to MP4/M4V files with h.264 video you should be fine. If you're keeping foreign language audio that might be where the bloat is. I usually keep all the audio through MakeMKV but strip out unneeded audio when I run it through handbrake.

You can get greater file size reduction if you trans-code to h.265, but note RaspberryPi's can't hardware decode it, but h.264 is probably a good place to start. Also if you want THE best compression/quality you have to use "Placebo" rate (slowest) in Handbrake. As for audio, I also strip out unwanted tracks in Handbrake, I'll often leave the orginal 5.1 and down mix a second track for Stereo.

This is diverging from topic, but I also recommend assigning multiple CPU cores to HandBrake process before starting your transcoding - cuts down on time and roughly load balance your system (i.e. take Handbrake off of CPU0).

Check out my replies in ChillyHellion, I don't know if you get notified for embedded replies, (if you haven't already) as I gave you a few extra bits of data. A few other tips also popped up to mind, since you're new (things I learned along the way).

  1. Does your source have the black top-bottom bars? If yes, look at "loose" and "auto" crop under cropping.
  2. If you're willing to sacrifice quality over file size under video you could change it to variable frame rate. However, if you want best quality file I would stick with constant frame rate & same as source; use Plex/Emby/Kodi to stream it or transcode on the fly if need be.
  3. Before you go hog wild with your movie collection look at, h.264, h.265, h.264 v. h.265 and decide what codex you want to use. [psa: I haven't watched full video on 3rd link]

You're welcome.

Digitizing is a word, but that term usually references an analog medium being turned into digital. Records to CD/MP3 or VHS to digtial-video. The correct term you're looking for is Transcoding - as you transitioning from one digital encoding to another.

Have fun and good luck.
